turns:
Project rules (always apply):
- Never run a destructive git command (reset --hard, clean -f, push --force, branch -D, checkout .). Prefer reversible operations; if a destructive one is truly needed, stop and confirm first.

This repo has no .gitignore. Add one covering the usual Python build and cache artifacts.

Rules relevant to this task:
- Before your first write, create a branch for the task and do the work there. Never commit to the default branch. Branch names follow type/kebab-description, where type is one of feature, bugfix, hotfix, chore, release, docs.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits: type(scope): subject, where type is one of feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, ci, build, perf, style.

events.command: ls -a && echo "---" && git status --short && echo "--- tracked files:" && git ls-files

git add .gitignore && git commit -m "chore(repo): add Python .gitignore

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>" && git log --oneline -2 && git status --short

events.text:
Added `.gitignore` on branch `chore/add-python-gitignore`, committed as `chore(repo): add Python .gitignore`.

Coverage: bytecode/`__pycache__`, C extensions, packaging/build/dist and egg-info, pip logs, test & coverage artifacts (pytest, tox, coverage, hypothesis), type-checker/linter caches (mypy, pyre, pytype, ruff), virtualenvs and `.env`, Jupyter checkpoints, and common editor/OS files.

One thing to be aware of: the packaging block includes `lib/` and `lib64/` (standard in the upstream GitHub Python template, for in-tree venv layouts). If you ever add a source directory named `lib/`, that rule would silently ignore it — worth dropping those two lines then. The three existing modules are top-level files, so nothing in the repo is affected today.
